title: Send and Sync
intro: Two questions decide whether a type may be used from more than one thread. `Send`: may this value be moved to another thread? `Sync`: may several threads hold a `&T` to it at once? The compiler answers both from the types and refuses the program when the answer is no. Together with the borrow rules, that check is how safe Rust has no data races, and it is why `Arc<Mutex<T>>` compiles across threads where `Rc<RefCell<T>>` does not.

coming_from.go: Go compiles a program that shares a plain variable between goroutines, and the race detector (`go run -race`) reports unsynchronized accesses it sees when the program runs. Rust asks at compile time instead, from the types: `Send` ("this value may move to another thread") and `Sync` ("a `&T` may be used by several threads"). There is no flag to switch it on.
coming_from.kotlin: Whether a class is safe to use from several threads is something you read in its documentation (the Java `ArrayList` page says it is not synchronized) or in an annotation such as `@ThreadSafe`, and `javac` checks neither unless you add a checker. `Send` and `Sync` put that fact in the type: the compiler works it out from the fields and refuses a call that hands the type to a thread it is not safe on.
coming_from.python: In the standard CPython build only one thread runs Python code at a time (the GIL), and that does not make "read the variable, then write it" atomic: the Python FAQ lists `i = i+1` as not atomic, and free-threaded builds have no such lock at all. Rust has no interpreter lock, and instead the compiler checks `Send` and `Sync` on every value that crosses to a thread.
coming_from.typescript: Worker threads do not share objects by default: `workerData` and messages are copies (unless you transfer an `ArrayBuffer`), and sharing is opt-in with `SharedArrayBuffer` and `Atomics`. Rust threads live in one address space and can share memory, so it needs a rule for which types may be shared: `Send` and `Sync`, checked at compile time.
coming_from.java: Thread safety is documentation or annotation: `ArrayList` says it is not synchronized and `ConcurrentHashMap` says it is, and `javac` checks neither (a checker such as Error Prone's `@Immutable` is opt-in). A Java data race has a limited set of allowed outcomes under the memory model, which is not the same as a correct result. In Rust safe code cannot have one, because `Send` and `Sync` are checked on every value a thread receives.
coming_from.csharp: The `List<T>` page says instance members are not guaranteed to be thread safe, and the compiler does not check that you respected it. `Send` and `Sync` are the same facts as traits the compiler works out and enforces: `Arc<Mutex<List>>` compiles across threads where a type holding an `Rc` does not.
coming_from.c: `pthread_create` takes a `void *`, so any pointer can go to any thread and nothing in the type says whether sharing it is safe. A data race is undefined behavior. `Send` and `Sync` are that missing information, written in the type and checked by the compiler.
coming_from.cpp: `std::thread` accepts any callable, including a lambda that captures a local by reference, and a data race is undefined behavior ([cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/multithread)). Rust's `Send` and `Sync` are checked on everything a thread receives, and a type with a non-atomic reference count, like `Rc`, is not allowed to cross.

notes: `Send` means a value may be moved to another thread. `Sync` means a `&T` may be shared between threads; the standard library defines it as "`T` is `Sync` if and only if `&T` is `Send`". Both are marker traits with no methods.

The compiler implements them for you, field by field: a struct is `Send` when every field is. One `Rc` anywhere inside makes the whole struct not `Send`, and the error names the chain from the thread call down to the `Rc`.

`thread::spawn` needs the closure and the thread's result to be `Send` (and `'static`). `Arc<T>` is `Send` only when `T` is `Send` and `Sync`: `RefCell<i32>` is not `Sync`, `Mutex<i32>` is, which is why the shared-counter pattern is `Arc<Mutex<T>>`.
Safe Rust has no data races, and it still has deadlocks and logic races. Two correct `lock()` calls with a gap between a check and the change compile, run, and give a wrong answer.

gotcha.title: A struct that holds an Rc, handed to a thread
gotcha.looks_fine: A job object holds a reference to a list that the main thread also uses. The worker adds to it while the main thread waits, and the main thread reads the list afterwards.
gotcha.rust_sees: `thread::spawn` needs everything the closure takes to be `Send`. The closure takes `job`, a `Job` holds an `Rc`, and `Rc` is not `Send`, so `Job` is not `Send` and the closure is not either. The error names that chain.
gotcha.why: The standard library says an `Rc` that two threads clone at the same time can corrupt its count, because the count is not atomic. Your program is fine: the main thread is waiting in `join`, so only one thread touches the count at a time. The compiler judges the type, not that argument, and the same shape without the waiting would be a data race. Swap the `Rc<RefCell<..>>` for `Arc<Mutex<..>>`, as `fixed.rs` does.

go.says: Go runs this and prints `log: ["resize"]`. The `Job` holds a pointer to the slice and the compiler does not ask which goroutines may use it. `go run -race` can report a race when two goroutines touch it without synchronization.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints the log. A `MutableList` is a plain `ArrayList`, which is not synchronized, and nothing stops you from handing it to a thread. It is correct here because of `join()`.

python.says: Python prints `log: ["resize"]`. Any object can be given to a thread, and the list is correct here because the main thread waits in `join()`.
python.code:
import json
import threading


class Job:
    def __init__(self, name, log):
        self.name = name
        self.log = log


def run(job):
    job.log.append(job.name)


log = []
job = Job("resize", log)
t = threading.Thread(target=run, args=(job,))
t.start()
t.join()
print("log:", json.dumps(log))

typescript.says: Prints `log: []`. A worker does not get the same object: `workerData` is a copy, so the worker changes its own list and the main thread's list stays empty. Nothing is shared unless you ask for a `SharedArrayBuffer`.

java.says: Java runs this and prints the log. The `ArrayList` is documented as not synchronized, and the compiler does not check how you share it. It is correct here because `join()` orders the worker's add before the main thread's read.

csharp.says: C# runs this and prints the log. `List<T>` is not guaranteed to be thread safe, and nothing enforces how you share it. It is correct here because `Join()` waits for the thread to finish.

c.says: C runs this and prints the log. The worker gets a pointer to a shared buffer, and nothing in the types says whether that is safe. It is correct here because of `pthread_join`.

cpp.says: C++ runs this and prints the log. A `shared_ptr` is safe to copy from several threads (its count is atomic in practice), but the vector inside is not locked. It is correct here because `join()` orders the worker's push before the main thread's read.

python.code:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

words = ["alpha", "beta"]

with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:
    # hand the list to a pool thread and get it back as the result
    back = pool.submit(lambda: words).result()
    print("moved there and back:", json.dumps(back))

    # two threads read the same list at once; nothing checks that this is safe
    a = pool.submit(lambda: len(words[0]))
    b = pool.submit(lambda: len(words[1]))
    print(f"lengths read in parallel: {a.result()} and {b.result()}")

import sys
import threading

print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
count = 0
N = 2_000_000


def work():
    global count
    for _ in range(N):
        count += 1  # read, add, write back


threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print("expected:", 4 * N)
print("got:     ", count)
